title: Spectral Audio Signal Processing — shard 1: Preface and Introduction through FIR Digital Filter Design

topics: Preface — purpose and audience: material developed for the CCRMA spectral-modeling course offered since 1984, aimed at beginning graduate students in computer music and engineering.

Preface — prerequisites and method: Fourier transforms, elementary digital signal processing, digital filtering, and linear systems support a computational treatment of spectral analysis, modeling, modification, and resynthesis.
Preface — Book Series Overview: dependency map placing this volume among related online books and showing which background texts support its advanced topics.

Introduction and Overview — spectral perception: the cochlea separates frequencies analogously to a prism, motivating Fourier-domain descriptions of timbre, source separation, formants, periodic signals in noise, speech consonants, and tonal music.
Introduction and Overview — Elementary Spectrum Analysis: finite records, the DFT, windowing, and the interpretation of magnitude spectra.
Introduction and Overview — Short-Time Fourier Transform and Time-Frequency Displays: repeated windowed transforms as the central analysis tool for nonstationary audio.
Introduction and Overview — Short-Time Analysis, Modification, and Resynthesis: spectral editing, overlap-add reconstruction, and the phase vocoder as the book's main processing arc.

Introduction and Overview — STFT Applications and Multirate Filter Banks: spectral modeling, time scaling, filter-bank views, polyphase structures, perceptual coding, and wavelets previewed for later chapters.
Chapter 2 — Fourier-transform taxonomy: DFT, DTFT, Fourier series, and continuous Fourier transform classified by finite/infinite and discrete/continuous time and frequency domains.
Chapter 2 — DTFT definition and interpretation: spectrum as inner products or projections onto complex sinusoids, with inverse synthesis over one 2π-periodic frequency interval.
Chapter 2 — continuous Fourier transform and inverse: transform pairs, convergence qualifications, and generalized-function treatment of idealized signals.
Chapter 2 — DTFT theorems: linearity, time reversal, conjugation and Fourier symmetry, shifts and linear phase, convolution, correlation, autocorrelation, and Parseval's power theorem.
Chapter 2 — multirate Fourier theorems: stretching by zero insertion, spectral repetition, downsampling and alias summation, antialias filtering, and rational L/M conversion.
Chapter 2 — differentiation and spectral roll-off: multiplication by time index corresponds to frequency differentiation; increasing endpoint smoothness accelerates asymptotic decay.
Chapter 2 — spectral interpolation: a finite record's DTFT is exactly interpolated from DFT samples by a periodic aliased-sinc kernel.

Chapter 2 — zero padding: denser sampling of the same underlying spectrum, FFT-friendly lengths, peak-display interpolation, zero-phase conventions, and prevention of time aliasing after spectral modification.
Chapter 3 — Rectangular Window: Dirichlet/asinc spectrum, narrow main lobe, fixed high sidelobes, Gibbs leakage, and the effect of increasing record length.
Chapter 3 — Generalized Hamming family: cosine taper as a sum of shifted rectangular-window spectra; Hann and Hamming endpoint, sidelobe, roll-off, and main-lobe tradeoffs.
Chapter 3 — MLT sine window: coding-gain optimum, minimum moment of inertia, transform coding, and time-domain alias cancellation with 50-percent overlap.
Chapter 3 — Blackman-Harris family and cos^P windows: multi-term cosine windows, shifted-spectrum implementation, and systematic endpoint-smoothness versus roll-off design.
Chapter 3 — Spectrum Analysis of an Oboe Tone: measured-record comparison under rectangular, Hamming, and Blackman windows, demonstrating leakage-limited weak-harmonic visibility.
Chapter 3 — preemphasis: approximately +6 dB/octave spectral flattening for voice and a practical leaky differentiator with a one-pole inverse.
Chapter 3 — Bartlett, Poisson, and Hann-Poisson windows: triangular convolution construction, exponential z-plane contraction, and monotone sidelobe-free decay for suitable Hann-Poisson parameters.
Chapter 3 — DPSS/Slepian window: maximization of energy concentration inside a prescribed main-lobe band via the principal eigenvector of a sampled-sinc Toeplitz matrix.
Chapter 3 — Kaiser window: modified-Bessel approximation to DPSS with a continuous beta parameter controlling time-bandwidth and sidelobe attenuation.
Chapter 3 — Dolph-Chebyshev window: minimax/equiripple sidelobe design, closed-form Chebyshev construction, length estimate, and endpoint-impulse risk.
Chapter 3 — Gaussian window: Fourier self-similarity, minimum second-moment time-bandwidth product, and quadratic log magnitude enabling accurate parabolic peak interpolation.
Chapter 3 — optimized windows: framing a window as a zero-passband lowpass FIR approximation, with perceptual, time-domain, monotonicity, and derivative constraints.
Chapter 3 — linear-programming window design: symmetric positive samples, normalized DC response, stopband bounds, minimax objective, and optional monotonicity or derivative regularization.
Chapter 4 — FIR-design framing: finite filters as approximations to desired frequency responses under explicit norms, constraints, transition widths, and perceptual priorities.
Chapter 4 — ideal lowpass filter: rectangular frequency response and its infinite, noncausal sinc impulse response.
Chapter 4 — lowpass specifications: passband ripple, stopband attenuation, transition bandwidth, dB-to-linear conversions, and why a nonzero transition band is indispensable.
Chapter 4 — naive least-squares truncation: exact time-domain truncation is L2-optimal by Parseval yet performs poorly when asked to approximate a discontinuous brick wall without transition freedom.
Chapter 4 — frequency-sampling FIR design: inverse DFT of sampled desired responses, intersample deviations, time aliasing, and verification with a heavily zero-padded FFT.

Chapter 4 — window method: multiply the ideal impulse response by a finite window; in frequency this convolves the desired response with the window transform and sets transition width by main-lobe width.
Chapter 4 — Kaiser bandpass example: empirical beta and length formulas, a 101-tap 20 kHz design, equal-transition-width limitation, and comparison with a Remez equiripple result.
Chapter 4 — Hilbert-transform design: analytic signals, positive-frequency retention, ±90-degree phase response, and ideal impulse response 1/(πt).

Chapter 4 — practical Hilbert transformer: half-sample centering avoids the singularity, symmetric transition bands force alternating zero taps, and a long frequency-sampled target is Kaiser-windowed to the final length.

Chapter 4 — generalized window method: smoothly interpolate an arbitrary desired response, choose or synthesize phase, inverse transform, verify energy concentration under the window, window, then compare achieved and desired spectra.

Chapter 4 — minimum-phase design: Hilbert-transform relation between log magnitude and phase, the cepstrum, causality, and reflection of unstable poles or nonminimum-phase zeros through the unit circle.
Chapter 4 — Lp optimal FIR design: weighted frequency-response error under L1, L2, and L∞ norms as a generally convex optimization in the coefficients.
Chapter 4 — Chebyshev/Parks-McClellan design: unique minimax weighted-error solution, equiripple alternation, efficient Remez exchange, and numerical convergence limits at high orders.

Chapter 4 — least-squares linear-phase design: even impulse-response symmetry reduces the response to a cosine basis; normal equations and the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse implement orthogonal projection.
Chapter 4 — Chebyshev design by linear programming: introduce a scalar error bound and minimize it subject to linear inequalities, trading Remez efficiency for more general constraints.

Chapter 4 — general and nonlinear-phase FIR design: complex desired spectra handled with real coefficients by stacking real and imaginary equations; examples include inverse, fractional-delay, polyphase, and minimum-phase filters.
Chapter 4 — convex and nonlinear optimization: second-order cone methods and general optimization tools extend FIR design to quadratic constraints and perceptually driven objectives.
key_results: Chapter 2, Fourier-transform taxonomy: the four standard transform cases are DFT (finite/discrete time and frequency), DTFT (infinite discrete time, continuous periodic frequency), Fourier series (finite periodic continuous time, discrete frequency), and FT (infinite continuous time and frequency).
Chapter 2, DTFT: X(ω)=Σ_n x(n)e^{-jωn}, with x(n)=(1/2π)∫_{-π}^{π}X(ω)e^{jωn}dω; the spectrum is 2π-periodic.

Chapter 2, Fourier interpretation: each transform value is an inner product with a complex sinusoid, so analysis measures projection and inverse transformation synthesizes the signal from those components.
Chapter 2, symmetry: for real x, X(-ω)=conj(X(ω)); consequently magnitude and real part are even, while phase and imaginary part are odd modulo phase wrapping.
Chapter 2, shift theorem: x(n-l) transforms to e^{-jωl}X(ω); delay changes only phase, adding a linear phase slope of -l.
Chapter 2, convolution and correlation: (x*y) transforms to XY, while cross-correlation transforms to conj(X)Y; autocorrelation therefore transforms to |X|².
Chapter 2, Parseval/power theorem: the time-domain inner product equals the corresponding normalized frequency-domain inner product, preserving energy across transform domains.
Chapter 2, stretch/repeat theorem: inserting L-1 zeros between time samples produces L spectral repetitions; str_L(x) corresponds to rpt_L(X).
Chapter 2, downsampling theorem: retaining every Mth sample gives Y(ω)=(1/M)Σ_{k=0}^{M-1}X(ω/M+2πk/M); overlap among these copies is aliasing, prevented by limiting the input to |ω|<π/M.
Chapter 2, rational resampling: conversion by L/M is conceptually upsample by L, lowpass-filter the spectral images/aliases, then downsample by M.

Chapter 2, Riemann roll-off: if a window has n derivatives with the appropriate bounded-variation smoothness, its transform decays asymptotically as O(1/ω^{n+1}); endpoint smoothness buys approximately another 6 dB/octave per order.

Chapter 2, exact spectral interpolation: the DFT samples uniquely specify the DTFT of a finite record through periodic aliased-sinc interpolation; computing an IFFT, zero-padding in time, and taking a longer FFT performs uniform interpolation exactly.
Chapter 2, zero-padding limitation: padding adds no signal information and cannot improve true resolution; it samples existing lobes more densely for display and peak estimation.
Chapter 2, zero-phase padding: a zero-centered sequence must place nonnegative times at the buffer start and negative times at the end; padding belongs between them, not after the apparent sequence.

Chapter 3, rectangular window: an M-sample zero-phase rectangle has W(ω)=sin(Mω/2)/sin(ω/2), first sidelobe near -13 dB, approximately 6 dB/octave sidelobe decay, and main-lobe width 4π/M between first zeros.
Chapter 3, window-length effect: increasing M narrows the rectangular main lobe but does not lower its relative sidelobes; leakage level is controlled by window shape, not record length alone.

Chapter 3, Hann window: the α=1/2 generalized-Hamming member has endpoint value and slope zero, first sidelobe about -31.5 dB, approximately 18 dB/octave decay, and a main lobe twice as wide as the rectangular window's.
Chapter 3, Hamming window: α=25/46≈0.54 nearly minimizes peak sidelobe in its two-term cosine family, reaching about -42.76 dB; nonzero endpoints restore a 6 dB/octave asymptotic roll-off.

Chapter 3, MLT sine window: when applied in both analysis and synthesis, its square is a Hann window; time-domain alias cancellation permits 50-percent overlap in transform coders such as MP3 and AAC.

Chapter 3, Blackman-Harris family: an L-term cosine window transforms into a sum of 2L-1 shifted rectangular spectra, permitting efficient frequency-domain smoothing; the classic Blackman has about -58 dB peak sidelobes and 18 dB/octave decay.

Chapter 3, oboe comparison: at the chosen durations, a rectangular window obscures upper harmonics with leakage, Hamming reveals more, and Blackman clearly reveals the harmonic series because its lower sidelobes accommodate the recording's large spectral dynamic range.
Chapter 3, Bartlett window: a triangle is the convolution of two rectangles, so its transform is a squared asinc; its main lobe is twice the rectangular width and its first sidelobe is about -26 dB.
Chapter 3, Poisson window: multiplying an impulse response by an exponential taper contracts its z-plane transfer function radially, H_P(z)=H(z/r), a useful system-identification interpretation.

Chapter 3, Hann-Poisson window: for decay parameter α at least about 2, magnitude decreases monotonically away from its peak, providing a nominally sidelobe-free objective useful for hill-climbing peak searches.

Chapter 3, DPSS optimum: the discrete prolate spheroidal sequence maximizes the ratio of spectral energy in a chosen main-lobe interval to total energy and is the principal eigenvector of a sampled-sinc symmetric Toeplitz matrix.

Chapter 3, Kaiser approximation: beta=0 yields the rectangle; with α=β/π, the first-null estimate is (2π/M)sqrt(1+α²), and widening by roughly one rectangular main-lobe unit buys about 25 dB of sidelobe reduction.
Chapter 3, Dolph-Chebyshev optimum: for fixed main-lobe width it minimizes maximum sidelobe level, producing equiripple sidelobes; an approximate length is 1+(2/ω_c)acosh(1/r).

Chapter 3, Gaussian uncertainty: the Gaussian transforms to a Gaussian and achieves the minimum second-moment time-bandwidth product σ_tσ_ω=1; its log magnitude is exactly quadratic, motivating parabolic interpolation.

Chapter 3, window optimization: minimax stopband design with linear equality/inequality constraints is a linear program; monotonicity and L1 or L∞ derivative penalties can suppress undesirable time- or frequency-domain behavior.
Chapter 4, ideal lowpass: H(ω)=1 inside |ω|≤ω_c and zero outside has h(n)=sin(ω_cn)/(πn)=2f_c sinc(2f_cn), which is infinite and noncausal.

Chapter 4, transition-band necessity: truncating a brick-wall ideal response to 30 or 71 taps yields only roughly 10 dB of stopband rejection and corner ringing, whereas granting a finite transition band enables a 71-tap Remez design beyond 60 dB; a useful scale is transition width at least about 4π/L.

Chapter 4, frequency-sampling warning: the inverse DFT exactly matches desired samples but may deviate badly between them and suffer time aliasing, so every design must be inspected with a much denser, zero-padded response grid.

Chapter 4, window method duality: time-domain multiplication by w convolves the ideal frequency response with W; achievable transition width is governed by the window main lobe and narrow passbands cannot be smaller than roughly half that width.

Chapter 4, Kaiser sizing: the empirical length law M≈(A-8)/(2.285Δω), paired with the standard piecewise beta estimate, converts attenuation and transition-width specifications into a practical first design.

Chapter 4, equal-transition limitation: a single window shape imposes essentially the same transition width at every band edge; unequal requested widths are therefore rounded toward the most demanding edge unless a more general optimization is used.

Chapter 4, analytic signal: the ideal Hilbert transformer has H(ω)=j for negative frequencies, 0 at DC, and -j for positive frequencies; x_a=x+jH{x} cancels negative frequencies and doubles positive ones.

Chapter 4, Hilbert kernel: the continuous ideal impulse response is h(t)=1/(πt), noncausal and singular at zero; a practical even-length design centers zero between samples, introducing a half-sample delay that must also be applied to the real path.
Chapter 4, Hilbert design economy: choosing transition bands symmetrically around one-quarter the sample rate forces every other impulse-response coefficient to zero, halving the filtering work.

Chapter 4, generalized window design: a fast noniterative sequence—smooth desired response, inverse FFT, verify concentration, window, FFT, compare—scales to thousands of taps and is suitable for interactive or adaptive frequency-response shaping.

Chapter 4, minimum phase from magnitude: for a minimum-phase H=Ge^{jΘ}, Θ is the Hilbert transform of ln G; equivalently the log spectrum is analytic and its inverse transform, the cepstrum, is causal.

Chapter 4, cepstral minimum-phase conversion: add each negative-time cepstral coefficient to its positive-time counterpart and zero the negative side; this reflects unstable poles and nonminimum-phase zeros inside the unit circle.
Chapter 4, Lp formulation: minimize ||W(ω_k)[H(ω_k)-D(ω_k)]||_p over FIR coefficients; p=2 gives least squares and p=∞ gives minimax/Chebyshev design, normally within a convex problem.

Chapter 4, Chebyshev optimum: the unique minimax solution has alternating equal-magnitude weighted-error extrema; Remez/Parks-McClellan converges monotonically in exact arithmetic but commonly becomes numerically unreliable beyond a few hundred taps.

Chapter 4, least-squares geometry: for an even zero-phase FIR, H is a cosine-series matrix A times the independent coefficients; the solution satisfies A^TAh=A^Td and is the orthogonal projection A A†d of the target onto A's column space.
Chapter 4, numerical least squares: solve the overdetermined system directly with a stable linear solver rather than explicitly forming the pseudoinverse or normal-equation inverse.

Chapter 4, complex-response fitting: a nonlinear-phase target with real coefficients is reduced to a real least-squares problem by vertically stacking Re(A), Im(A) and the corresponding real and imaginary desired-response samples.

Chapter 4, method tradeoff: window/frequency-sampling methods are fast, robust at very high orders, and naturally drooping; Chebyshev methods use taps more efficiently with equiripple bands and tighter transitions but cost much more design time and can fail numerically.
pedagogy: This shard teaches from Fourier duality and executable design intuition rather than from theorem-proof formalism alone. Smith introduces a physical or auditory motivation, derives the relevant transform relation, then repeatedly turns it into short MATLAB/Octave procedures and heavily zero-padded verification plots. Chapter 2 is compact mathematical review: transform definitions and theorems are stated and derived with enough detail to support later manipulation, while practical indexing and FFT-buffer conventions receive unusual emphasis. Chapter 3 is comparative and empirical: each window is judged by main-lobe width, peak sidelobe, asymptotic roll-off, time-bandwidth, and suitability for a signal task, culminating in the same measured oboe recording under three windows and then optimization formulations. Chapter 4 moves from an intentionally bad ideal-response truncation to progressively more capable methods—frequency sampling, window design, Hilbert and minimum-phase constructions, Lp optimization, Remez exchange, least squares, linear programming, and complex-response fitting. Worked code is integral to the exposition, and warnings about numerical convergence, inconsistent software conventions, time aliasing, and visually under-sampled FFTs are treated as core knowledge. The assumed learner already knows Fourier transforms, elementary DSP/filtering, linear systems, calculus, and complex arithmetic. Exercises and referenced problems are present throughout the online book, but this shard's strongest reusable pedagogy is its cycle of derive, implement, inspect, compare, and explain the failure mode.

gems: Introduction, Motivation: the ear is compared to a prism because the cochlea spatially separates sound by frequency; the analogy immediately turns Fourier analysis from abstract decomposition into a model of hearing.
Introduction, Motivation: Hubble's discovery of galactic redshift is used as a vivid example of extracting physical meaning from displaced spectral lines.

Chapter 2, Fourier Transform as Projection: transform analysis is described as 'measuring how much' of each complex sinusoid is present, a reusable bridge from vector inner products to continuous spectra.

Chapter 2, Zero Padding Example: a 21-point Hamming window is shown with no padding, 2× padding, and dense references; two samples per lobe look improved, but 10× still visibly misses details while 100× and 1000× become indistinguishable.

Chapter 2, Zero Padding: the text distinguishes five legitimate uses—radix-friendly FFT length, smooth displays, peak interpolation, room for spectral modifications, and avoiding time aliasing—from the false claim of added resolution.
Chapter 3, Generalized Hamming: the familiar Hamming constant is not arbitrary; 25/46≈0.54 nearly reaches the family's Chebyshev optimum, with -42.76 dB versus the theoretical -43.19 dB minimum.

Chapter 3, Hamming Use Case: approximately 40 dB sidelobe suppression is tied to 'one-percent accurate' systems and roughly 8-bit telephone-codec quality, translating a window plot into an engineering tolerance.

Chapter 3, MLT Sine Window: applying the sine window twice squares it into Hann, and time-domain alias cancellation makes the resulting 50-percent overlap a practical coding construction used in MP3/AAC.

Chapter 3, Oboe Figures 3.16-3.18: two periods with a rectangular window, four with Hamming, and six with Blackman form a memorable controlled experiment in which only the lowest-sidelobe choice clearly reveals all upper harmonics.

Chapter 3, Voice Preemphasis: the approximately -6 dB/octave spectral tilt of voiced sound motivates a +6 dB/octave differentiating prefilter; the practical leaky form 1-0.95z^-1 retains an easy one-pole inverse.
Chapter 3, Hann-Poisson: a window can deliberately trade the usual lobe pattern for a monotone magnitude slope, turning spectral peak finding into a friendlier hill-climbing or convex-search problem.
Chapter 3, Kaiser Rule: increasing the main-lobe width by about one rectangular-window unit buys roughly 25 dB of sidelobe reduction, a compact mental estimate for beta/time-bandwidth tradeoffs.

Chapter 3, Dolph-Chebyshev Warning: the mathematically optimal equiripple sidelobes may create conspicuous impulses at the window endpoints, translating a frequency-domain optimum into audible pre/post echoes.

Chapter 3, Gaussian Peak Fitting: because Gaussian magnitude is quadratic in dB, three-point parabolic interpolation is exact for an ideal Gaussian lobe and often improves real spectral peak estimates.

Chapter 4, Bad Ideal Lowpass: a 71-tap truncated sinc still achieves only about 10 dB stopband rejection when no transition is allowed, whereas the same length exceeds 60 dB once a 0.5π-to-0.6π transition is specified.

Chapter 4, Kaiser Bandpass: a requested 20 kHz design with unequal transitions exposes a structural limitation—window designs want every transition to have the same main-lobe width—so one edge must be renegotiated.

Chapter 4, Hilbert Design: placing the 1/(πt) singularity halfway between samples simultaneously avoids infinity and produces the half-sample delay that an analytic-signal implementation must match in its real branch.
Chapter 4, Hilbert Symmetry: centering equal transition bands around fs/4 forces every other tap to zero, turning a symmetry observation into a factor-of-two computational saving.

Chapter 4, Kaiser versus Remez Hilbert Filter: the window design scales to thousands of taps and is almost instantaneous but wastes coefficients on passband overdesign and stopband droop; Remez roughly halves the transition width but takes orders of magnitude longer and fails near this 257-tap scale.

Chapter 4, Minimum Phase via Cepstrum: the recipe 'fold negative quefrencies onto positive ones, then zero the negative side' provides an implementable counterpart to the abstract statement that log magnitude and phase are Hilbert-transform pairs.

Chapter 4, Least-Squares Geometry: an overdetermined filter design becomes the literal orthogonal shadow of the desired response on the realizable cosine-basis subspace, making the normal equations visually inevitable.

Chapter 4, Optimization Choice: the chapter repeatedly shows that the norm is the design—L2 spreads error, L∞ controls the worst ripple, while added time-domain or derivative constraints encode artifact risks that a frequency-only optimum misses.
chapter_map: Course motivation, audience, prerequisites, and the full spectral-audio arc -> Preface; Introduction and Overview.
Transform-domain taxonomy and DTFT/FT conventions -> Chapter 2, Fourier Transforms and Theorems; Discrete Time Fourier Transform; Fourier Transform and Inverse.
Linearity, symmetry, shift, convolution, correlation, Parseval, multirate, and differentiation identities -> Chapter 2, Fourier Theorems for the DTFT; Continuous-Time Fourier Theorems.
DFT-to-DTFT interpolation, zero padding, zero-phase indexing, and FFT display practice -> Chapter 2, Spectral Interpolation.
Leakage fundamentals and the main-lobe/sidelobe tradeoff -> Chapter 3, The Rectangular Window; Generalized Hamming Window Family.
Hann, Hamming, MLT sine, Blackman-Harris, and frequency-domain cosine-window implementation -> Chapter 3, Generalized Hamming Window Family; Blackman-Harris Window Family.
Measured window selection for audio harmonics and preemphasis -> Chapter 3, Spectrum Analysis of an Oboe Tone.
Special-purpose windows and their constructions -> Chapter 3, Bartlett, Poisson, Hann-Poisson, Slepian/DPSS, Kaiser, Dolph-Chebyshev, and Gaussian sections.
Window optimization under minimax, monotonicity, and derivative constraints -> Chapter 3, Optimized Windows; Optimal Window Design by linprog.
Ideal lowpass response, engineering specifications, and why transition bands matter -> Chapter 4, The Ideal Lowpass Filter; Lowpass Filter Design Specifications; Least-Squares FIR Filter Design.
Frequency-sampling and classical window-based FIR workflows -> Chapter 4, Frequency-Sampling FIR Filter Design; Window Method for FIR Filter Design.
Kaiser sizing, multiband limitations, and Remez comparison -> Chapter 4, Window Method for FIR Filter Design, especially the Kaiser bandpass example and comparison to optimal Chebyshev FIR design.
Analytic signals and practical Hilbert-transform FIR construction -> Chapter 4, Hilbert Transform Design Example, including Primer on Hilbert Transform Theory through Conclusions.
Arbitrary-response fast FIR construction -> Chapter 4, Generalized Window Method.
Minimum-phase response from magnitude and causal cepstra -> Chapter 4, Minimum-Phase Filter Design; Minimum-Phase and Causal Cepstra.

Lp norms, Chebyshev/Remez, least squares, linear programming, complex responses, and convex optimization -> Chapter 4, Optimal FIR Digital Filter Design and all subsections through Nonlinear Optimization in Matlab.
